correctness.rationale: For the ordered normals with correlations a,b,c, trace(M^T M)=a^2+c^2+(b-ac)^2 by inserting the last rank-one loss after the first two projections. The exterior square of each plane projection is the rank-one projection on its normal, so the exterior-square product is ac u_k u_i^T. Its squared Frobenius norm yields the product p=a^2 c^2 of the two possibly nonzero squared singular values (zero ranks included). Thus the sum is Q+p and the product p. The sweep is strictly contractive by norm equality for orthogonal projections and independence of the three normals. With 0<Q<1 the feasible p range is contained in [0,(1-sqrt(1-Q))^2]; implicit differentiation shows the larger root decreases strictly since its derivative is (lambda_+-1)/sqrt((Q+p)^2-4p), with the endpoint handled by continuity. Ordering by the largest adjacent product covers zeros and ties; all-orthogonal sweeps vanish. Trace(M)=a^2+b^2+c^2-abc and trace of the exterior square is abc; cyclic shifts and transpose reversal also independently show the six spectra agree. The quadratic identity yields lambda_+<=Q, and lambda_+>= (Q+p)/2>Q/2 for p>0; for p=0 and Q>0 one has lambda_+=Q. For the independent star family in the record the endpoints have 2t^2 and the middle order has t^2+O(t^3), which proves the sharp nonattained sqrt(2) supremum. Inspected check.py without executing it: its invariants are rational, but its separate numerical ordering tests use approximations and do not establish strict monotonicity.

evidence: Yu–Diakonikolas give an exact fixed-order matrix and the exact norm-loss operator for arbitrary consistent systems. Their example of an exact norm on p. 14 is a special planar family with even m>=8. Hansen–Hochstenbach discuss order dependence, including an example with changed spectral radius. Dax discusses the heuristic of maximizing adjacent orthogonality; the survey discusses slow convergence with highly coherent consecutive rows.
broader_coverage.reasoning: An exact operator for each order gives the input for a fixed-order evaluation, but does not select the minimizing order or quantify the maximal within-instance ordering penalty. The other comparisons use different regimes or convergence objectives.

evidence: The prior norm-loss formula and Gram identity give the squared sweep norm as the squared norm of L^(-1)(L-I) in the nonsingular square case, with L the normalized unit lower Gram part. For three rows its strict lower-triangular entries are a,c,b-ac, so the standalone scalar formula is a direct evaluation of the prior operator. All six spectra agree by cyclic shifts and transpose reversal regardless of that evaluation.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The distinguishing work is comparing the resulting roots for the same Q and different adjacent products, proving the precise strict and tie behavior, and identifying the sharp uniform ratio and a full-rank approaching family. Those are not provided by the evaluated fixed-order representation or the spectral invariance alone.

originality.rationale: Credit the exact Gram-based sweep operator to prior work and the order-invariant spectrum to elementary cyclic-permutation and transpose identities. The supported distinct claim is the exact one-sweep minimizer for arbitrary independent triples, including ties, together with the sharp global comparison of best and worst orders on the same instance. The literature and catalogue statements inspected do not give that comparison or a stronger order-selection theorem that yields it as a special case.
residual_risks: Bounded searches cannot rule out an older equivalent projection-product ordering theorem or a sharp comparison under different notation; no general priority claim is made.

value.rationale: The least-sized nonsingular setting in which a sweep has genuinely different ordering choices has an exact worst-direction optimizer that need not follow conventional low-coherence heuristics. The equality of eigenvalues explains why spectral-radius analysis misses this initial effect, and the sharp ratio quantifies the maximum benefit of changing the order on one instance. This has value for the explicitly motivated one-sweep objective, not as a general recommendation for asymptotic convergence.
